t: Car Fleet II: Collision Times with Right-to-Left Fleet Analysis
o: Cars occupy strictly increasing positions and never overtake; a faster car behind eventually rear-ends whatever is ahead unless that entity escapes or merges into something even slower first. After contact, cars fuse into one fleet moving at the slowest member speed, so each car only cares about its FIRST contact ahead. Example 1: car 0 (speed 2) catches car 1 (speed 1) at t=1; car 1 alone catches nothing; car 2 (speed 3) catches car 3 at t=3. Example 2 shows cascading merges: car 0 ties car 1 in speed yet collides at t=2, because car 1 first merged into slower traffic ahead and slowed down. Positions go up to 10^5, so an efficient sweep matters.
k: Process right-to-left: by the time car i is considered, the fate of everything ahead is fully resolved.
Car i catches the entity led by car j at t = (pos_j - pos_i)/(speed_i - speed_j), valid only if speed_i exceeds that fleet speed AND t is no later than that fleet own crash deadline.
A monotonic stack discards fleets car i can never catch in time, leaving exactly its first contact on top.

a.i: Fill crash[i] from right to left. To find car i first collision, scan j = i+1, i+2, ... treating each car j as the current head of traffic ahead with deadline crash[j]; the first j passing the catch condition is the answer. This is correct because a car cannot physically bypass an unmerged catchable leader - the earliest valid j yields the earliest meeting time. Too slow for n = 10^5, but the clearest way to internalize the condition before adding the stack.
s: Iterate i from n-2 down to 0.
For each j > i compute deadline = infinity if crash[j] = -1 else crash[j].
If speed_i > speed_j and (pos_j - pos_i)/(speed_i - speed_j) <= deadline, set crash[i] to that time and stop scanning.
a.t: O(n^2) - each car may rescan every car ahead; fine as intuition, too slow for n = 10^5

a.i: Maintain a stack of surviving fleets as triples (position, speed, crashTime), built right-to-left. For the current car, pop every top it can never catch in time: the top is at least as fast (no closure ever), or the computed catch time exceeds the top crash moment (that fleet dissolves into deeper entries first). Whatever survives on top is the first contact; push the car with its newly derived crash time, or infinity when it never crashes. Every entry is pushed and popped once, giving linear time.
s: Iterate i from the last car to the first with an empty stack.
While the stack top exists and (speed_i <= top.speed or catch time > top.crash), pop it.
If the stack remains, crash[i] = (top.pos - pos_i)/(speed_i - top.speed); otherwise crash[i] = -1.
Push (pos_i, speed_i, crash[i] if finite else infinity).
a.t: O(n) - each fleet enters and leaves the stack at most once
a.sp: O(n) - the stack of pending fleets

w: Go straight to the stack in interviews and derive the catch condition aloud; justify popping with example 2 (car 0 skips car 1 because car 1 merges into slower car 2). Pitfalls: dividing by zero or a negative gap when the leader is faster (guard speed_i > fleet speed first), using strict inequality at deadlines (simultaneous collisions must count), and float precision (answers tolerate 1e-5, doubles suffice). Follow-ups: report collision positions or fleet sizes, or handle cars entering the road mid-simulation - the same fleet machinery applies.
